questions.q: What is the single fact that most fundamentally distinguishes smart contract CI/CD from web app CI/CD, per this lesson?
options: Smart contracts can't be tested automatically
Deployed contract bytecode is (without a proxy) immutable — there's no hotfix or rollback once it's live
Smart contracts don't need a build step
Web apps never need static analysis
questions.explain: Once CREATE/CREATE2 puts bytecode on-chain, it's permanent — unlike a web app, there's no quick hotfix or revert for a live contract without a proxy pattern.

questions.q: Why does this immutability push all of a contract pipeline's checks to run BEFORE the deploy transaction?
options: Because running checks after deployment is technically impossible
Because there's no "fix forward" option — a missed edge case after deployment can be a permanent exploit with real funds at stake
Because GitHub Actions only supports pre-deploy hooks
Because gas costs are lower before deployment
questions.explain: With no safety net after deployment, every correctness, security, and gas check has to be a gate the deploy can't pass without clearing first.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which of the following is NOT listed as something the pre-deploy pipeline must catch?
options: Correctness via fuzz/invariant/fork tests
Static analysis for known vulnerability patterns
Gas regressions via the gas snapshot check
Automatic rollback of a live mainnet contract
questions.explain: Automatic rollback of a live contract isn't a thing without a proxy — the lesson's whole point is that the pipeline has to catch problems before deployment, since there's no rollback after.

questions.q: Why can a contract that compiles cleanly and passes every local test still behave differently once actually deployed?
options: Local tests always use the wrong Solidity version
Deployment introduces real variables local testing doesn't have — actual gas price, block conditions, and the real state of contracts it interacts with
Compiling and testing are the same step and can't diverge
Deployed contracts run on a different EVM than local tests
questions.explain: Local tests run under conditions you control; a real deploy hits real gas prices, real block state, and real external contract state — exactly the gap fork testing (Lesson 4) is built to close.

questions.q: What does "ship fast, fix forward" describe, and why doesn't it apply to live smart contracts?
options: It's a Foundry command, and it doesn't apply because Foundry doesn't support it
It's the web-app assumption that bugs can be patched quickly after shipping — it doesn't apply because a live contract (without a proxy) can't be patched at all
It's a Git branching strategy only used for testnets
It's a gas optimization technique
questions.explain: "Ship fast, fix forward" assumes a bug can be quickly patched post-release — an assumption that breaks down for immutable, already-funded contract code.
